messages.subject_clean: JOB: PostDoc in Statistics, U. of Kent, Canterbury, UK
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

We are currently advertising the following postdoctoral position in
statistics. Please feel free to contact me for further information. With
apologies for cross-postings.

Best regards,
Mark.

UNIVERSITY OF KENT AT CANTERBURY

INSTITUTE OF MATHEMATICS AND STATISTICS

RESEARCH ASSOCIATE IN STATISTICS

A Research Associate (RA1A) post in Statistics in the
Institute of Mathematics and Statistics at the
University of Kent at Canterbury is available from
1st September 2000 or such a date as may be arranged.

In particular, the position is aimed at undertaking research
in spatial statistics with the newly appointed Professor Mark Steel.
The latter research will involve the development of statistical models
for (marked) point pattern data and Bayesian inference procedures
for dealing with substantive applications to environmental problems.
As both the theoretical complexity of the models involved and the
size of the available data make such applications quite challenging,
particular emphasis will be on efficient computational algorithms and
implementations, using e.g. recently developed Markov chain Monte
Carlo methods. Issues of model choice and model uncertainty will
be investigated in detail.

The successful applicant will be expected to have a strong
research potential and an enthusiasm for developing both
theoretical work and serious applications. This appointment will
be for a fixed term of two years.

The successful candidate will ideally have a Ph.D. in statistics
or a related field. Previous experience in working with spatial
models or environmental data will be valued. Familiarity with
computers and some exposure to modern computational methods is
certainly important, but a strong theoretical background might partly
compensate for that.

Informal enquiries should be directed to Mark Steel, who is
currently still at the University of Edinburgh, and can be reached at
Tel : +44 (0)131-650 8352 (direct line), Fax: +44 (0)131-650 4514,
E-mail: Mark....@ed.ac.uk. Website: http://www.ed.ac.uk/~msteel/

Information about the Institute of Mathematics and Statistics
can be found on the World Wide Web at http://www.ukc.ac.uk/IMS/

Depending on experience and qualifications, salary will be
in the range £16,286 - £24,479.

A copy of the Further Particulars is available on the IMS website
at http://www.ukc.ac.uk/IMS/jobs/index.html or can be obtained by
telephoning the Personnel Office on +44 (0)1227-827837 (24 hours)
or +44 (0)1227-823674 (Minicom), quoting reference A00/75.

Closing Date: 30 June 2000.

The University is committed to implementing its Equal Opportunities
Policy.

messages.subject: Re: multiple species
messages.body_plain:
> > Using DISTANCE is it possible to enter and analyze data from a general
> > Breeding Bird Survey (Point Transect with two intervals:  less than 50 m and
> > greater than 50 m) in which more than one species may be encountered at each
> > point?

Yes - but you have to supply a nominal maximum distance, e.g. 250m.  This
is because Distance evaluates all integrals numerically, so it can't
integrate to infinity.  The distance should be a distance beyond which
detections are unlikely - but don't make it excessively large, as Distance
might then fail to converge.  You may want to choose a larger value for
larger, more detectable species.

Note that you will only be able to fit one parameter models
(e.g. half-normal without adjustment), and you will have no information to
assess the fit of that model.  If you want to do analysis outside
Distance, you'll find formulae on p175 of the distance sampling book
(http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distancebook/).

Handling multiple species is straightforward.  Either set up a project per
species, or more simply, create an extra field at the observation level
corresponding to species.  Enter a species code in this field for each
detection, then poststratify by species, or select a species at a time in
the data filter.

Steve Buckland

I have tried to send the following to the Distance list, but it has been
rejected twice. I am not sure what I am doing wrong, but perhaps you can
help.  Thank you.

A portion of my line transect study of dolphins involves a small
population(#30) resident to a bay. I realize that line transect is not the
most appropriate method to follow such a small population, but as I have the
data I would like to see the best possible results that can be derived. My
understanding is that the best AIC is generally recommended as the criterion
for model selection, but I also understand that AIC assumes a large sample,
and perhaps for this population is not the best criterion. Knowing the
population size, the results with the lowest CV appear to be the most
reasonable. I realize that CV is not generally recommended as a criterion
for model selection, but wonder if this is ever appropriate. I would
appreciate input. Thank you. Linda-Jane Smith

I will be performing spotlight counts of white-tailed deer using distance
sampling.  In my lit. search so far, I have not seen mention of methods for
using distance sampling on serpentine 'transects' (I will use a vehicle on
mountain roads).  I have only seen methods for straight transects.  I am
looking for references that address this question.
TIA,

messages.subject: Re: novice question
messages.body_plain:
> > I will be performing spotlight counts of white-tailed deer using distance
> > sampling.  In my lit. search so far, I have not seen mention of methods for
> > using distance sampling on serpentine 'transects' (I will use a vehicle on
> > mountain roads).  I have only seen methods for straight transects.  I am
> > looking for references that address this question.

There is a good reason for this ... we strongly discourage use of roads
for transects!  It is rare for animal density along roads to be
representative of overall density - and rarer still to be able to
demonstrate that this is so.  Further, you can't even assume that road
transects will give you a useful relative measure of abundance, as traffic
may increase over time, or hunter activity vary with time, leading to
varying densities along roads that do not reflect variation in the wider
population.

However, if you plan to do it anyway, you should look at

Quang, P. X. and Becker, E. F. (1999) Aerial survey sampling of contour
transects using double-count and covariate data, in \em Marine Mammal
Survey and Assessment Methods\em (eds G. W. Garner, S. C. Amstrup,
J. L. Laake, B. F. J. Manly, L. L. McDonald and D. G. Robertson), Balkema,
Rotterdam, pp. 87--97.

The issues addressed by Quang and Becker for contour transects will apply
also to road transects.

Lex Hiby has also looked at the issue of curved transects - in his case,
they are transects through rain forest, where existing paths are used.  I
don't think his work is published yet.

You should also look at the following paper:

Gill, R. M. A., Thomas, M. L. and Stocker, D. (1997) The use of portable
thermal imaging for estimating deer population density in forest
habitats. Journal of Applied Ecology, 34, 1273--86.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: novice question
messages.body_plain:
While studying chameleons in Madagascar we have attempted to compare curved
transects (ie. set along trails) and straight (i.e. non-trail) transects.
Some preliminary data is published in Oryx:

Jenkins, R. K. B., Brady, L. D., Huston, K., Kauffmann, J. L. D.,
Rabearivony, J., Raveloson, G. and Rowcliffe, J. M. (1999) The population
status of chameleons within Ranomafana National Park, Madagascar and
recommendations for future monitoring. Oryx, 33, 38-46.

To summarise, we found that densities of species were different between the
two transects - usually higher along trails. There are many possible reasons
for this, but ultimately we concur with the general view that trails are
best  avoided.

---------------------------------
Dr. Lee Brady

The Durrell Institute of
Conservation and Ecology,
University of Kent,
Canterbury,

messages.subject: Re: novice question
messages.body_plain:
We have been using distance sampling to estimate deer density in a number of forest areas using thermal imaging. There are several comments I can make about the problem of using roads:

We usually only work from small forest roads that are not open to the public.
There appears to be much more avoidance from public roads (though I havent yet tested them for significance)

We have been using thermal imaging because it can detect deer at greater distances, even if partly hidden in vegetation, and doesn't cast a beam which the deer can see. Even so, we have still had problems with avoidance in some instances. In most cases it seems to be avoidance of the observer (not the road) because results have often been better on subsequent occasions once the importance of minimising disturbance is made clear to the observer. This can be done minimising speed and by focussing on the road ahead, (rather than at right angles into the forest), because deer close to the road sometimes walk away when they hear a vehicle coming.

We tried alternatives to forest roads - one was to try cutting paralell transects from a random starting point and walking these, but the we found (apart from the additional cost) that visibility was much more restricted from a narrow path than from a road, so we have not tried these again. Attempts to walk through the forest off paths always created more disturbance than from a road, so were worse.

Another concern with roads is that they may not penetrate all habitats within the area - this is more likely in mountainous terrain. Further, the terrain itself  affects visibility, because animals are more easily detected on opposing valley slopes than on the observer's slope.

In summary, using roads can give good results, but only with care and under certain circumstances. It would clearly be preferable to avoid them altogether, but that may be completely impractical. Any methods that can be devised to control for the various limitations and biases involved would clearly be very useful. I would have thought that GIS would be a useful tool to support the design and analysis of surveys (and could provide covariates) but I'm not aware of any attempts yet to combine them with distance sampling. Any ideas or suggestions would be welcome!

Robin Gill
Forest Research

messages.subject: Re: novice question
messages.body_plain:
We have been using distance sampling to estimate deer density in a number of forest areas using thermal imaging. There are several comments I can make about the problem of using roads:

We usually only work from small forest roads that are not open to the public.
There appears to be much more avoidance from public roads (though I havent yet tested them for significance)

We have been using thermal imaging because it can detect deer at greater distances, even if partly hidden in vegetation, and doesn't cast a beam which the deer can see. Even so, we have still had problems with avoidance in some instances. In most cases it seems to be avoidance of the observer (not the road) because results have often been better on subsequent occasions once the importance of minimising disturbance is made clear to the observer. This can be done minimising speed and by focussing on the road ahead, (rather than at right angles into the forest), because deer close to the road sometimes walk away when they hear a vehicle coming.

We tried alternatives to forest roads - one was to try cutting paralell transects from a random starting point and walking these, but the we found (apart from the additional cost) that visibility was much more restricted from a narrow path than from a road, so we have not tried these again. Attempts to walk through the forest off paths always created more disturbance than from a road, so were worse.

Another concern with roads is that they may not penetrate all habitats within the area - this is more likely in mountainous terrain. Further, the terrain itself  affects visibility, because animals are more easily detected on opposing valley slopes than on the observer's slope.

In summary, using roads can give good results, but only with care and under certain circumstances. It would clearly be preferable to avoid them altogether, but that may be completely impractical. Any methods that can be devised to control for the various limitations and biases involved would clearly be very useful. I would have thought that GIS would be a useful tool to support the design and analysis of surveys (and could provide covariates) but I'm not aware of any attempts yet to combine them with distance sampling. Any ideas or suggestions would be welcome!

Robin Gill
Forest Research
Alich Holt Lodge
Wrecclesham
Surrey GU10 4LH
01420 22255

messages.subject: NoviceQues.,Part2
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to all who replied to my message.  I appreciate the input.  Some
additional points I should have mentioned:
1.  I realize that density near the road may not reflect overall density.
The point of this study is to determine the most practical, not necessarily
most accurate, method. We know there is the way things should be done and
the way they are done.
2.  In this case, 97% of the forest is in 1 forest type (different
silvicultural treatments throughout, will be sampled in proportion to
availability).
3.  I'll be comparing the results of spotlighting to pellet group counts and
automatic camera estimates (both conducted throughout the forest), so I
should see how near-road vs. interior densities relate.  This may allow for
use of spotlight data as a covariate predictor.
4.  There will be >100 marked deer present, so mark-resight data gathered
during distance sampling will also show how road vs. interior densities
compare.
Any other thoughts?
Thanks Again,
CL

messages.subject: Re: novice question - GIS
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 22 May 2000 12:12:01 +0100 (BST), Robin Gill wrote:

> >I would have thought that GIS would be a useful tool to support the design
and analysis of surveys (and could provide covariates) but I'm not aware of
any attempts yet to combine them with distance sampling. Any ideas or
suggestions would be welcome!

We at St Andrews are working on a new version of program Distance (version
4). Distance 4 will include an automated survey design tool based on the GIS
component MapObjects (by ESRI - uses shapefiles like ESRI's ArcView) and the
work of one of the PhD students here, Samantha Strindberg.  The design tool
lets you generate survey plans based on various designs, and also does
simulations to look at things like coverage probabilities etc.  You can
easily print off maps of the survey plans, etc.  We will be using a
preliminary version of this software at the advanced distance workshop in the
fall (see http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distanceworkshop/)

In the future, we will be using the GIS tool to extend the functionality in
Distance to include spatial modelling of density (PhD work at St Andrews by
Sharon Hedley).  There will also be simulation capabilities which will allow
you to simulate populations of animals in space and look at the performance
of different designs combined with different abundance estimators.

The new version of distance will be on general release around November or
December this year, and will be free to download for non-commercial use.  The
GIS-automated design component will be in this release, but we are at present
not sure about the spatial modelling component: depends on time and funding
constraints.  We have been funded these past 3 years by two UK research
councils, but this grant has now finished.  I will be making an announcement
on the list shortly seeking sponsors for future development of Distance.

Cheers,

 - Len Thomas

messages.subject: DST & Habita Selection
messages.body_plain:
Dear DISTANCE listserver,

We sampled sika deer along a route including several habitat types. We
measured deer's perpendicular distances, and can calculate deer density
for each habitat using distance sampling theory. Now, we want to analyze
habitat selection of sika deer using the estimated deer density of each
habitat. We plan to use the estimated deer density and the strata width
to give estimated deer number for each habitat, and then to analyze
habitat selection by Bonferroni test. However, we do not know it is
applicable or not, and hope someone tell us any other better method?

Any advice or comments are appreciated.
Thank you.

Yuchun Li
